title: Making the game is 30% of it
author: McTraderLLC
selftext: I've noticed a lot of ai game 'developers' here have intention of making profit out of their games. I hate to sound negative but cold hard reality is that making the game is the fun and "easy" part of the whole process. Unless you have a super innovative game with luckiest timing to go viral with barely any marketing expense, it won't get any attention. Make sure to have a strategic plan on how you will promote it FIRST and have a very big marketing budget to compete with the semi/big boys. Of course there are couple that will take off with barely any ad/marketing dollar spent, but those talented developers probably only used Ai to assist them, not just vibe code the whole ass game suddenly with no prior history in this field. And if you're game is vibe coded, just remember anyone else can too if there really is potential in the game, with big marketing budget on top of that.

comments.author: Navadvisor
comments.body:
On the other hand it doesn't make sense to market a bad game, I don't think you can outrun a bad game with good marketing. Maybe that can work once or twice for a big studio with a lot of brand loyalty, but that's really just cashing in on the value of your brand in the worst way possible.

I think more difficult than marketing, once you have a good game marketing it becomes less of an uphill battle, is play testing and QA and holding yourself to a high development standard. You can one shot a GTA clone but look a little bit at it and it's trash, it has some of the basic mechanics but to make the huge story and make it balanced and fun and progress well, and iron out all the rough edges, that's going to take a lot more time, a lot a lot more time.

I disagree. I barely do any marketing and I do great. Instead, I'd split it:

- 30% making most of the game. The exciting bit, where the ai is blasting out stuff.
- 20% marketing the game. Making all the posts and ads and stuff
- 50% finishing the game. All the boring stuff, ensuring performance. Balancing various bits. Localisation. Polishing UI art. This takes SO LONG and AI does almost nothing to help.

Again, I'd love to hear if anyone has a reliable solution because I'd use it!

replies.author: drallcom3
replies.body:
I used gemma-4-26b (any lower and it's not good enough) for some mods and it translated even difficult pieces perfectly fine. Gemma/Gemini is best for text work. Since I speak several languages I was able to verify English to some more complex language. It helps a lot if you design your loca files with AI in mind. Make a header that tells the model that this is a game and some details about the game. You can add comment lines before entries if you sense it can't be translated easily. I even made a tool where I can specify the reading level etc.

Anyone saying it's not good enough probably doesn't want it to be good enough.

replies.author: lyeeedar
replies.body:
Gemma does a really bad job of translation to Chinese, and it's bad at following rules. I actually use it as a fast pre-translate, but it constantly makes critical errors like translating things literally (so, reading as nonsense in the target language because it's just word for word), failing to translate parts (leaving English) or failing to follow other rules like maintaining placeholders.

Note, this is on a corpus over over 6 million words so maybe at smaller scales the errors aren't noticeable.

replies.author: drallcom3
replies.body:
> Note, this is on a corpus over over 6 million words so maybe at smaller scales the errors aren't noticeable.

I haven't tried such extreme cases. LLMs in general struggle with large context and especially local models (make sure you don't use gemma-12b or something similar) work better with small contexts.

Might be that it's worse at novel style translations. I was only using it for games that don't have novel style strings.

> like translating things literally (so, reading as nonsense in the target language because it's just word for word), failing to translate parts (leaving English) or failing to follow other rules like maintaining placeholders

I never had those problems though. Might be that your model was too poor or your setup confused it.

replies.author: TMiyoshi
replies.body:
It can do a lot of work but it will definitely make mistakes. As with everything, you're supposed to verify the output, but unlike other aspects of gamedev, you can't really do this yourself. 

AI will also default to "textbook" terminology, instead of actual gaming lingo. 

If you expect to just click a button to translate everything into 20 languages and call it done, I have bad news.

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48
comments.body:
I have 28 years of experience as a professional software engineer with 16 of them in the game industry. I could have made 3x or more my salary if I had gone into fintech or something (I had plenty of opportunities) and I also released 4 indie games, tried and failed to build more than a dozen others over several decades and made a grand total of something like $130 USD on my indie efforts.

Success in games was a lottery before AI and it's just more of one now - and increasing your chances often involves making what the market wants not what you do.  In my not so humble opinion if you're making games for any reason besides you can't NOT make them you're doing it wrong.  This doesn't mean ignore promotion and marketing but if profit is your primary motivation you're way better off with B2B than games.

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color

I'm curious about the indie games you tried and "failed" at.  

Some of the most enjoyable games I've ever played have mostly been indie games and sharing a common theme, mainly that the developers seems to not give a fuck about the recipe for making a successful game and just do their thing and go all out on it. 

Most of these are not really small projects either (like project zomboid, kenshi, rimworld etc), these titles would probably make a project manager pull their hair out I'm guessing.

replies.author: Relevant-Positive-48
replies.body:
When I say games I tried and failed at I mean games I spent more than 6 months on and that never got released.  For a few examples (not going to dox myself with specifics):

1.  A potential funding deal for one of them fell through and the team fell apart.  
2. A project that was too big for me to finish on my own fell apart when the other programmer and the lead artist got married and decided they didn't have time for the game.  
3.  I stopped working on a game when the job I took in the industry had me working 16 hours a day 6 days a week and I never picked the indie game back up when I was done with that particular job.

comments.author: darkoblivion000

I am making a game because I love the idea of the design in my head. I love the process of iterating over and over again to figure out if the concepts work, how to make it better, look better, feel better. If no one buys my game I will be disappointed and I will learn that my taste apparently sucks lol but I will have made my ideas into a digital polished form. And I will have fun with my own game.

It’s like any other skill or craft that I decide to put time into improving - there’s internal and external reinforcement cycles.

Money is a consequence. Perfect the craft and the money will follow. People who want to one shot something and throw it on the store will not understand this concept.

comments.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
comments.body:
Here are the facts:

* The more you let AI do, the more likely anyone can do it exactly like you
* Your game will be part of AI's training and anything "new" discovered or built will end up back in the training and used in other people's implementation
* If you have no skills in dev or art, then there is a very strong likelihood your game will be no different than most other games.
* If you have an "original" idea it can be cloned, almost instantly and be competing against you in very short time.

In short, it creates an environment of hyper competition. Where only truly exceptional people will succeed. And I think the irony of that is the exceptional people.

comments.author: EnormousHorseman
comments.body:
Market first was bad advice in 2012. Indie devs only have so many hours to spend. If you have a separate sales partner that is free or profit share absolutely market first.

Otherwise you'll spend so much time and money marketing a vertical slice you'll never finish your game.

I tried the market first strategy and lost my shirt and never finished my game. This is a a philosophy that only fits teams with dedicated salesmen, it's a huge energy drain for creators that lack sales skills and guarantees burnout.
